correctness.rationale: The cited source fixes the reset threshold and unique target of every shortest word. Reading a shortest word backward from that target and rotating the preimage set converts the two letters into a deterministic scheduled Boolean system: \(b\) is a no-op, while \(a\) copies the membership bit at offset \(q-p\). Coprimality makes that dependency map one cycle. The first possible creation times are \(1,1+p,\ldots,1+(q-2)p\); missing any such forced copy delays it by a full \(q>p\) steps and makes completion by the known threshold impossible. Exactly \(q-1\) positions therefore force \(a\). Before the last creation the sole present state whose dependency successor is absent is the initial endpoint, producing exactly \(p-1\) forced \(b\)-positions. At every other position the compared bits agree, so either letter has identical reverse action and the choices are independent. Subtracting the forced positions from \(L=pq-2p+1\) leaves \((p-1)(q-3)\) free bits, giving exactly \(2^{(p-1)(q-3)}\) shortest reset words. The actual verifier exhaustively checks all coprime pairs through \(q=13\) and symbolically checks the schedule through \(q=100\); these checks support but do not replace the all-parameter schedule proof.
residual_risks: The theorem is only for the \(n=q\) Wielandt-type subfamily with coprime cycle lengths.

value.rationale: The Wielandt-type automata are a standard slowly synchronizing family, and shortest-word multiplicity is a natural refinement of reset threshold: it measures how rigid the extremal synchronization mechanism is. The exact exponential count for every coprime parameter pair is structural, not a finite census, and the reverse-preimage schedule is reusable for related two-cycle families.
residual_risks: The proof exploits a special two-edge structure and does not yet extend to the full \(W(n,q,p)\) family.
